tagline: Turn raw CVEs into what an attacker would do with them.
lore: Orthrus, the two-headed dog and brother of Cerberus — here he links two worlds: your vulnerability findings and the attacker's ATT&CK playbook.
problem: A CVE number says something is broken, not what an adversary does with it. Detection engineers think in ATT&CK techniques and tactics; vulnerability data arrives without that context, so two teams look at the same finding in two languages.
does: Orthrus fetches the public ATT&CK-to-CVE mapping from MITRE's Center for Threat-Informed Defense, matches it to the CVEs in your findings, and shows the techniques and tactics your unpatched estate enables on an ATT&CK matrix. He tags the affected assets with each CVE's primary impact, secondary impact and exploit technique.

glance.caption: Orthrus's At a glance on the bundled sample navi.db: 3 assets whose findings cite a CVE in the public ATT&CK mapping, 5 techniques across 4 of 15 tactics — the coverage is only as wide as the public mapping.

capabilities: the Center for Threat-Informed Defense ATT&CK→CVE mapping, fetched after you approve it (or auto-approve in Settings), with a bundled snapshot offline.
by default only CVEs present in navi.db, so every tag lands on real assets.
techniques and tactics your findings enable, by mapping type; full screen and email from the widget.
Mitre : Primary Impact: <technique>, Secondary Impact: <technique> and Exploit Technique: <technique> on the assets carrying each CVE, via navi's tag-by-CVE.
not every CVE has a mapped technique; an unmapped CVE simply gets no Mitre tag.

run over one tag's assets (an owner, a tier, an environment): the ATT&CK exposure, matrix, planned tags and ACR > 7 list cover only that tag, and tags written from that view land only on its assets. Switch between the whole estate and your last 5 tags without re-running.
how: Orthrus reads CVEs from your local navi.db and joins the public mapping. Tags use `navi enrich tag --cve` — the CVE picks the assets — with the category fixed to Mitre, behind the write gate and a confirm.
who: Threat-informed defense programs mapping exposure to techniques, and detection engineers who want to know which techniques their unpatched estate enables.
better: Laelaps says a vulnerability is exploited; Orthrus says how it's used. Fenrir labels each attack-path step with its ATT&CK technique, Nemesis counts ATT&CK techniques in its score, and Covenant re-applies the Mitre tags on its schedule.
different: not another threat feed to read — labels on the vulnerabilities you already track.
vulnerability management and detection engineering sort the same list the same way.
every technique comes from the public mapping.
cta: Ask Orthrus what your vulnerabilities let an attacker do.
